cards.title: Model markup at low and high price points, including future bulk costing
cards.summary: Estimate cost per unit and profit per unit across the plausible price range so a single bad price assumption does not sink the business.
cards.use_when: You have a rough price band and a first cost estimate and need to see whether the product can carry your expenses.

cards.title: Launch with exactly one SKU and treat extra variants as complexity debt
cards.summary: Minimize SKUs at launch because each variant adds inventory capital, storage cost and shipping-error risk.
cards.use_when: You are deciding how many sizes, colors or formulations to launch with.

cards.title: Judge subscription fit by real consumption rate, not category type
cards.summary: Subscriptions are desirable but only work when the customer genuinely repurchases often enough to justify the cadence.
cards.use_when: You are evaluating whether a product can support recurring revenue and lower blended acquisition cost.

cards.title: Screen size, weight and shipping cost before you commit
cards.summary: Oversized or heavy products create shipping costs that deter buyers or eat margin, so estimate carrier costs on rough dimensions early.
cards.use_when: You are comparing product concepts and shipping economics matter to your margin.

cards.title: Design for durability to cut returns, breakage and refunds
cards.summary: Durability covers both packaging and product formulation, and directly reduces returns and in-transit damage.
cards.use_when: You are choosing materials, packaging or formulation for a shippable physical product.

cards.title: Map seasonality to protect cash flow
cards.summary: Identifying seasonal demand swings with Google Trends lets you plan inventory buys and marketing calendar around cash flow.
cards.use_when: You are validating a product whose demand may cluster in specific months, or planning inventory and ad budgets.

cards.title: Prioritize products that solve a pain or serve a passion
cards.summary: Products tied to a real problem or an active hobby make customer acquisition easier than nice-to-have items.
cards.use_when: You are ranking several viable product ideas and want a qualitative tiebreaker on marketability.

cards.title: Favor consumable and disposable formats for repeat business
cards.summary: Consumable products naturally generate repeat purchase and open the door to subscriptions and better lifetime value.
cards.use_when: Choosing between otherwise comparable product ideas, or building a retention plan.

cards.title: Check shelf life and perishability before stocking inventory
cards.summary: Perishable goods risk dead stock and write-offs if sales are slow, so verify shelf life against your realistic sell-through window.
cards.use_when: You are evaluating food, cosmetics or any product with an expiry or degradation risk.

cards.title: Research regulations and restrictions before investing in a category
cards.summary: Food, cosmetics, baby products and similar categories carry compliance requirements that should be identified before you spend on sourcing.
cards.use_when: Your product idea touches regulated categories or you are unsure whether claims, labelling or testing rules apply.

cards.title: Close validation with a written highlights-and-concerns summary
cards.summary: End the framework by stating what is working and what is not, so the decision to proceed is explicit rather than assumed.
cards.use_when: You have completed the sixteen validation questions and need to make a go/no-go call or justify one to a partner.

cards.title: Filter Ad Spy Tools for Proven, Facebook-Scaled Winners
cards.summary: Exact Get Hooked filter stack for surfacing validated, older-demographic Facebook winners.
cards.use_when: Configuring an ad-spy tool such as Get Hooked to find products that already have proven spend and scale behind them.

cards.title: Product Criteria: Daily Problem Plus Retail Absence
cards.summary: Two baseline criteria — a problem that recurs daily and no big-box retail availability — for screening product ideas.
cards.use_when: Screening candidate products before spending on creative, site build or inventory, especially in health and wellness.

cards.title: Native Ad Scouting on News Publisher Widgets
cards.summary: Use paid-content widgets on weather and news sites to surface recurring, older-demographic health offers.
cards.use_when: Sourcing product ideas and native-ad angles aimed at a 60+ audience outside of ad spy tools.

cards.title: Cross-Validate With the Free Facebook Ad Library
cards.summary: Use Ad Library image filtering and run-time checks as a free substitute for a paid ad spy tool before committing.
cards.use_when: Validating a shortlisted product and checking whether competitors are already running native-style image ads.

cards.title: Mine the Longest-Running Ad for the Winning Angle
cards.summary: Extract the marketing avatar and message from a validated product's longest-running creative and reuse that angle.
cards.use_when: You have a validated product with a history of running ads and need a starting creative angle before building your own.

cards.title: Prioritize Facebook Over TikTok/Instagram Burner Scouting
cards.summary: Deprioritize TikTok and Instagram burner-account scouting in favor of Facebook-based and tool-based research.
cards.use_when: Deciding where to spend product-research hours, particularly as a beginner without a trained dropshipping eye.

cards.title: Market-First Product Research Hierarchy
cards.summary: Choose a passionate market and an emotional problem before picking a product, because market and problem drive sales more than the product itself.
cards.use_when: Starting a new ecommerce product search, or when a previous product test failed and you're tempted to jump straight to product hunting.

cards.title: Use Claude to Generate Winning Emotional Sub-Niches
cards.summary: Prompt Claude (Opus or Sonnet) to produce a list of emotional sub-niches downstream from your chosen market, then pick five to research further.
cards.use_when: You have picked a market and want a fast list of specific emotional problems to build products and offers around.

cards.title: Connect Get Hooked to Claude via MCP for Ad-Library Sourcing
cards.summary: Wire the Get Hooked ad-aggregator MCP server into Claude as a custom connector so the AI can pull live competitor brand and ad data.
cards.use_when: You want Claude to research real competitor brands, active ads, angles and funnels instead of relying on its training data alone.

cards.title: Run the MCP Product-Sourcing Prompt Over Your Five Sub-Niches
cards.summary: Feed the MCP-connected Claude a prompt with MCP usage instructions plus your five chosen sub-niches to return qualifying brands, pain points, ad patterns and funnels.
cards.use_when: Claude is connected to the Get Hooked MCP and you have narrowed to five emotional sub-niches.

cards.title: Estimate Competitor Revenue with the SimilarWeb Formula
cards.summary: Reverse-engineer a competitor's monthly revenue floor as monthly visits × estimated conversion rate × estimated AOV, and require roughly $200k–$300k+/month before treating them as proof of a winning product.
cards.use_when: Validating whether brands surfaced by your ad-spy research are actually selling at scale.

cards.title: The Two Golden Margin Rules: 3x COGS and $30 Gross Margin
cards.summary: Require at least 3x cost of goods sold at retail price and at least $30 of gross margin per unit so the product can absorb rising Meta ad costs.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether a sourced product can support paid acquisition before committing to a test.

cards.title: Diagnose a Failed Product Test: Ads Problem or Funnel Problem
cards.summary: After a failed test, ask 'why' and split the cause into ad-related issues (CPC/CTR/CPM) or funnel-related issues (ATC, checkout completion, AOV) before abandoning the product.
cards.use_when: A product test underperforms and you're deciding whether to kill the product, fix creatives, or fix the funnel.

cards.title: Ad Failure KPIs: CPC, CTR and CPM Thresholds
cards.summary: Use link CPC above $1.50, CTR below 3%, and CPM above $80 as indicators that a failed test is an advertising problem, usually a creative problem.
cards.use_when: A US product test is unprofitable and you need to determine whether the ads, not the offer or product, are the constraint.

cards.title: Funnel Failure KPIs: ATC Ratio, Checkout Completion and AOV
cards.summary: Use landing-page-to-add-to-cart below 10%, ATC-to-purchase below 30%, and AOV under a 20–40% markup over base price as indicators that the failed test is a funnel problem.
cards.use_when: Ad metrics look acceptable but the product still isn't converting, or you need to locate friction between click and purchase.

cards.title: Keep AI Sourcing and Ad Execution in Separate Ownership
cards.summary: AI-assisted sourcing ends at a validated, margin-checked product; creative, media buying and storefront work are separate disciplines that determine whether the product actually succeeds.
cards.use_when: Scoping a product-research sprint, or setting expectations that finding the product is only one part of a profitable launch.

cards.title: A job is progress in a circumstance, not a customer type
cards.summary: Define jobs as the functional, social and emotional progress someone seeks in a specific circumstance, rather than as demographic segments.
cards.use_when: Starting any avatar or customer-research effort and deciding what unit of analysis to research and record.

cards.title: Mine five sources for undiscovered jobs
cards.summary: Find jobs by looking in personal life, nonconsumption, workarounds, negative jobs and unusual uses rather than asking customers for feature ideas.
cards.use_when: When you need new job candidates rather than validation of existing assumptions or feature wishlists.

cards.title: Prioritize passive struggle data over active operational data
cards.summary: Favor observations of customer struggle over sales and customer-attribute reports, which are easier to collect but describe outcomes rather than causes.
cards.use_when: When choosing what evidence to gather and when a data-driven team wants to substitute reports for direct research.

cards.title: Map the forces: push and pull versus habits and anxieties
cards.summary: A purchase happens when the push of the struggle and the pull of the new solution outweigh the habits of the present and the anxiety of the new.
cards.use_when: When diagnosing why prospects stall or abandon, or when building objection-handling into an avatar record.

cards.title: Interview by reconstructing the purchase timeline
cards.summary: Interview technique that traces the chain of triggers and events leading to a decision instead of asking about product attributes or satisfaction.
cards.use_when: Running customer interviews to uncover the job and the trigger moment behind a purchase.

cards.title: Distinguish the Big Hire from the Little Hire
cards.summary: Separate the purchase decision from the actual use and repeat-use decision, because a good job on the buying side does not guarantee retention.
cards.use_when: When diagnosing whether problems sit in acquisition or in onboarding, activation and repeat usage.

cards.title: Build the job spec: tradeoffs, competition and obstacles
cards.summary: A job spec is the résumé of experiences a solution must deliver, defining which tradeoffs the customer accepts, what alternatives must be beaten, and what obstacles must be removed.
cards.use_when: After a job is identified, when translating it into requirements for product, offer or messaging.

cards.title: Storyboard the customer's struggle
cards.summary: Visualize the sequence of a customer's struggle and choices to expose where the current situation breaks down and where your solution enters.
cards.use_when: Synthesizing interview material into a shared internal view of the job before writing avatar records or messaging.

cards.title: Give every avatar quoted evidence
cards.summary: A non-negotiable baseline for avatar records: direct quotes from research that support the job, the trigger and the objections.
cards.use_when: Writing or reviewing avatar records, especially when tempted to summarize without evidence.

cards.title: Inventory candidates before fixing the number of avatars
cards.summary: Research should produce a discovered set of jobs from interviews and observations rather than a predetermined count of personas.
cards.use_when: Planning avatar research and deciding how many distinct avatars to maintain.

cards.title: Use negative jobs as an opportunity lens
cards.summary: Tasks people dread doing are strong job candidates because removing an unpleasant obligation is a clear progress worth paying for.
cards.use_when: When hunting for new offers or messaging angles, especially in categories where customers complain about the process rather than the product.

cards.title: Diagnose a stalled decision with the competing-solutions list
cards.summary: Identify every alternative the customer weighed, including doing nothing and DIY fixes, to find which one actually wins and why.
cards.use_when: When conversion is weak or customers describe long deliberation before buying.

cards.title: Capture trigger moments as discrete, datable events
cards.summary: A trigger is a specific event that made the status quo unacceptable, and pinpointing it beats recording vague motivations.
cards.use_when: When your avatar or messaging lacks urgency and prospects agree with the message but never act.

cards.title: Treat habits of the present as the silent competitor
cards.summary: The customer's existing routine and defaults block change even when the new solution is clearly better, so map the habit before assuming desire is enough.
cards.use_when: When prospects acknowledge the problem and the solution yet fail to switch.

cards.title: Study nonconsumption to find latent demand
cards.summary: People who buy nothing in the category are a rich source of jobs because their current coping mechanisms reveal unmet progress.
cards.use_when: When the existing market is crowded and growth requires serving buyers the category has never reached.

cards.title: Use unusual uses as a research probe, not an instant segment
cards.summary: Off-label and edge-case uses point to jobs the product was not designed for; validate the recurring pattern before acting on it.
cards.use_when: When reviewing support tickets, reviews or usage data and finding customers using the product in unexpected ways.

cards.title: Avoid persona theater: no demographic avatars without a job
cards.summary: Avatars built from demographic fields or fictional characters with stock photos do not explain behavior and should not be produced.
cards.use_when: When reviewing existing persona documents or when a stakeholder asks for an age-and-income-based avatar template.

cards.title: Ask what the customer fired, not only what they hired
cards.summary: The job includes what the customer stopped using, and knowing what got dismissed shows the tradeoffs and loyalties at stake.
cards.use_when: When mapping the competitive set and understanding what switching away from a solution really costs the customer.

cards.title: Jobs Theory: Innovation Built on Causality, Not Correlation
cards.summary: Christensen's core argument that customers 'hire' products to make progress in a specific circumstance, and that this causal job — not demographics or product attributes — predicts innovation success.
cards.use_when: Framing an innovation or product strategy, or when your team's data is descriptive (who buys, what they look like) but cannot predict which new offer will succeed.

cards.title: The Milk Shake Study: Circumstance Interviews Beat Attribute Surveys
cards.summary: How a fast-food chain discovered two different jobs for the same milk shake by observing buyers and probing what else they hired instead, and why asking customers to improve the product produced zero sales change.
cards.use_when: Designing customer research for a product with flat or declining sales, or when survey feedback ('cheaper, chunkier, chewier') is producing changes that don't move the number.

cards.title: Jobs Interviews: Track the Timeline of Triggers, Not Product Attributes
cards.summary: The interview method for surfacing a job: reconstruct the causal timeline of what happened before a purchase and avoid questions about the product's features.
cards.use_when: Building avatars, running win/loss or purchase interviews, or briefing an agency or researcher before qualitative fieldwork.

cards.title: Push, Pull, Anxiety and Habit: The Forces Behind a Purchase Decision
cards.summary: A decision to change happens when the push of frustration plus the pull of the new solution outweighs the anxiety about the new and the habit of the present — useful as the diagnostic frame for avatar research.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing why prospects stall mid-funnel, or structuring interview notes and avatar definitions around what actually triggered and blocked a switch.

cards.title: What to Skip: Demographic Personas and Feature-Wish Surveys
cards.summary: Christensen's explicit list of research artefacts the jobs method rejects, and what to do instead.
cards.use_when: Auditing an existing avatar or persona deck, or approving a research brief, to check it is built on causal evidence rather than demographics.

cards.title: Why Big Data and Customer Satisfaction Metrics Miss the Point
cards.summary: Data that groups customers by similarity or reports satisfaction cannot explain why a purchase happened, and assuming it can leads to churning out mediocrity.
cards.use_when: When a dashboard of demographics, market share and CSAT is being used as the basis for a product or growth decision.

cards.title: Avoid Innovating Toward 'Average': The Jagged-Profile Lesson
cards.summary: The US Air Force cockpit case, retold by Christensen, shows that a design fitted to the average user fits nobody — a direct argument against averaging segment needs into one solution.
cards.use_when: When a roadmap item or landing page is being designed to 'work for everyone', or when multiple jobs are being averaged into a single offer.

cards.title: Rewrite the Competitive Set as a Résumé of Alternatives
cards.summary: For any job, list every product the customer might hire and what each is good at, including items in entirely different aisles or categories, to see the real market size.
cards.use_when: Doing competitive analysis, sizing an opportunity, or repositioning a product that looks like a commodity inside its own category.

cards.title: From Broken Category Assumptions to Growth: Disruption vs Jobs
cards.summary: Disruption explains how incumbents respond to threats but does not say where to look for growth; Jobs Theory is offered as the offensive complement.
cards.use_when: Choosing the strategic frame for an innovation programme, or when a disruption lens has identified a threat but produced no product roadmap.

cards.title: Why Smart Managers Fail: Processes Perfectly Designed for Mediocrity
cards.summary: Great managers following all the best advice can still lead firms to the top and off a cliff, and the 'stupid manager' explanation collapses when a whole industry falls at once.
cards.use_when: Post-mortems where leadership failure is the assumed explanation, or when building an innovation process that you expect to produce breakthroughs.

cards.title: Recognising a Job: Little and Big, Predictable and Sudden
cards.summary: Jobs arise from situations; classifying them by size and predictability helps a team notice which jobs its product could plausibly be hired for.
cards.use_when: Generating job hypotheses in a workshop before doing timeline interviews, or mapping where an offer might fit into a customer's day.

cards.title: It's Not Just About Jobs: Experiences and Integration Create the Moat
cards.summary: Identifying the job is only the start; competitors can copy products but not well-integrated experiences, which is where sustained advantage sits.
cards.use_when: Planning what happens after a jobs insight is validated — turning it into a blueprint, an experience and internal process change.

cards.title: Define a job as progress in a circumstance
cards.summary: Jobs Theory defines the unit of innovation as the progress a person seeks in a specific circumstance, not a product category or customer type.
cards.use_when: When framing a new product, offer or campaign and you need to state clearly what the customer is actually trying to accomplish rather than describing features or audience demographics.

cards.title: Film the mini-documentary to characterise a job
cards.summary: Five prompts turn a vague customer struggle into a fully specified Job to Be Done by imagining a filmed episode of the customer's struggle.
cards.use_when: When you need to flesh out a job for messaging, product design or an interview guide and the usual demographic or needs-based descriptions feel empty.

cards.title: Use jobs theory to redraw your competitive landscape
cards.summary: Competition should be defined by everything the customer could hire in the same circumstance, not by products the industry buckets together.
cards.use_when: When assessing competitors, setting positioning, or feeling that your market is a zero-sum fight among near-identical products.

cards.title: Diagnose why needs- and trends-based innovation fails
cards.summary: Needs, trends and guiding principles are too general to predict a purchase; jobs are specific enough to build an innovation blueprint.
cards.use_when: When a product or campaign built around an important-sounding need or a trend has stalled, or when reviewing an innovation brief that lacks circumstantial detail.

cards.title: Ask 'what has to prove true' before committing resources
cards.summary: Discovery-driven planning forces teams to surface and test the assumptions behind a new initiative before large investment locks them in.
cards.use_when: When approving a new product, channel or market entry, or when projections look attractive but rest on untested beliefs.

cards.title: Apply Jobs Theory only where a real struggle exists
cards.summary: Jobs Theory is not universal; it stops being useful when existing solutions are good enough or the decision is purely rational and calculable.
cards.use_when: When deciding whether to run a jobs-based research project or whether another method (efficiency analysis, price modelling) is the better tool.

cards.title: Use theory as a causal lens, not a formula
cards.summary: Good theory tells you how to think about causes and produces if-then predictions you can test, unlike borrowed best practices.
cards.use_when: When diagnosing an innovation problem, teaching a team to reason about customer choice, or when results from industry best practices are inconsistent.

cards.title: Look outside the four habitual innovation lenses
cards.summary: Most managers organise innovation around product attributes, customer characteristics, trends or competitive response - all insufficient for predicting behaviour.
cards.use_when: When reviewing an innovation or marketing brief and deciding whether the framing is likely to predict customer choice.

cards.title: Learn from Toyota: design defects out with if-then process tests
cards.summary: Treating each defect as an anomaly to be root-caused and designed out of the process beat the Detroit approach of inspecting and reworking.
cards.use_when: When a repeatable process (fulfilment, creative production, onboarding) keeps producing errors that get patched rather than prevented.

cards.title: Recognise the legacy process that produces what you don't want
cards.summary: US automakers unwittingly designed a process highly effective at producing costly, inconsistent cars - a warning about the systems behind your outcomes.
cards.use_when: When outcomes are consistently poor or unpredictable and the reflex is to add patching steps rather than redesign the process.

cards.title: Reframe a market by serving non-consumption
cards.summary: SNHU found its biggest opportunity not by beating local colleges but by serving adults who otherwise would have done nothing.
cards.use_when: When your category looks saturated and growth has stalled under a one-size-fits-all offer aimed at the 'average' customer.

cards.title: Use a jobs lens to separate functional from experience-based buying
cards.summary: Prospects may ask about practical features while actually hiring you for a social and emotional experience, and the two require different offers.
cards.use_when: When designing a landing page, tour or sales conversation and deciding which elements actually drive the decision.

cards.title: Map competition as a shifted landscape, not a finite share fight
cards.summary: Seeing competition through jobs changes who you benchmark and how you innovate, from supply-side selling to demand-side responding.
cards.use_when: When your strategic plan assumes growth must come from taking share from direct rivals in a fixed market.

cards.title: Accept that the job endures while solutions change
cards.summary: Jobs are discovered, not created, and the underlying job stays stable even as the way people solve it changes dramatically.
cards.use_when: When evaluating a new technology or channel and wondering whether it changes the customer's need or just the means of solving it.

cards.title: Convert jobs insight into experience and process requirements
cards.summary: A layered job usually cannot be satisfied by a product alone; it demands a bundle of integrated experiences, which is where defensibility comes from.
cards.use_when: When moving from research findings to designing the full customer experience, including post-purchase and service layers.

cards.title: Run leadership questions to test customer understanding
cards.summary: A short question set checks whether you actually know why customers choose you and who you are really competing with.
cards.use_when: When preparing a strategy review, onboarding a team, or stress-testing a positioning statement.

cards.title: One-size-fits-none: segment by job, not by customer category
cards.summary: Serving distinct job-based segments with a single averaged solution fails everyone; separate them and rebuild each journey.
cards.use_when: You have multiple customer types (e.g., first-time buyers vs. repeat bulk buyers) receiving the same onboarding, offers or support flow and growth has stalled.

cards.title: Job-hunting method 1: mine your own life for jobs
cards.summary: Unresolved jobs in your own daily life are legitimate innovation territory; your life is articulate data.
cards.use_when: You need an innovation hypothesis and have no budget for formal research, or you're a founder/operator building for a market you personally belong to.

cards.title: Job-hunting method 2: hunt nonconsumption, not competitor share
cards.summary: People who use no solution at all — not competitors' customers — often hold the largest growth opportunity.
cards.use_when: Your category looks mature, saturated or price-competitive, and you suspect existing market-size data can't see untapped demand.

cards.title: Job-hunting method 3: read workarounds as demand signals
cards.summary: Compensating behaviors show customers who want a job solved badly enough to build their own solution.
cards.use_when: You're scanning for unmet needs and notice customers jury-rigging spreadsheets, manual processes or odd substitutes.

cards.title: Job-hunting method 4: negative jobs — what customers don't want to do
cards.summary: Jobs framed as 'I don't want to X' are often the richest opportunities, especially where the alternative is time-consuming and anxiety-laden.
cards.use_when: You're evaluating service design, flow simplification or any category where customers tolerate a painful routine.

cards.title: Job-hunting method 5: unusual uses reveal hidden jobs
cards.summary: Customers using your product off-label are showing you jobs your category doesn't acknowledge — and new revenue lines.
cards.use_when: You have a long-established product, flat growth, and suspect you're defined by a category rather than by what customers are doing with it.

cards.title: Sell the outcome, not the course catalog: B2B job alignment
cards.summary: When the buyer's job is to matter internally, sell subscriptions and owned outcomes around their business goals rather than discrete products.
cards.use_when: You sell to a functional buyer (HR, L&D, IT, marketing ops) whose internal credibility depends on connecting your product to executive priorities.
